summaries.example: Maya plans to bake cookies. She believes she must turn on the oven first, but she does not plan to turn it on. Her thoughts do not fit together well. She could change her plan, change her belief, or decide to turn on the oven. The important point is that her attitudes clash, even before we ask whether baking cookies is a good idea.
summaries.summary: Structural rationality is the idea that our mental states should fit together in suitable ways. Mental states include beliefs, intentions, and preferences. For example, it seems puzzling to believe that great cooks never overcook eggs, believe that you are a great cook, and also believe that you overcooked the eggs. It also seems puzzling to plan to do something while believing that a certain step is necessary but refusing to plan that step. Philosophers call these kinds of problems structural irrationality. They distinguish them from substantive rationality, which asks whether a belief or plan responds properly to the reasons and evidence a person has. A person might have an unsupported belief without having beliefs that clash. The entry also explains that philosophers disagree about the details: some think rationality mainly requires coherence, while others think it also requires responding to reasons. They debate whether requirements concern a whole combination of attitudes or one attitude in particular, whether they apply at one time or across time, and whether they govern mental states or the processes by which we form them. Finally, they ask whether structural rationality itself gives us a reason to be rational. No single answer has settled all these questions.
key_ideas: Structural rationality is about how a person’s thoughts and plans fit together.
A person can have a strange or poorly supported belief without being structurally irrational. The problem may arise when beliefs clash with one another.
One example is believing two things that cannot both be true.
Another example is planning a goal while refusing to plan a step the person believes is necessary for that goal.
Philosophers disagree about what all cases of structural irrationality have in common and whether structural rationality gives us reasons to change.
summaries.why_it_matters: Our beliefs and plans guide what we do. If they do not fit together, we may become confused, make poor plans, or fail to follow through. Studying structural rationality helps us ask whether the problem is a bad belief, a bad plan, or simply a conflict between them. It also teaches us to separate two questions: “Do my thoughts fit together?” and “Do my thoughts respond well to the reasons and evidence available to me?”

important_terms.definition: When a person’s beliefs, plans, or other mental states fit together in a sensible way.
A kind of rationality about whether a person’s mental states fit together.
A judgment about whether someone’s choice responds well to the reasons they have.
A mental state such as a belief, plan, wish, or intention.

questions_to_think_about: Can two beliefs disagree while each one seems reasonable by itself?
If a plan and a belief clash, which one should a person change?
Is it always wrong to believe everything that follows from another belief?
Why might people care about having thoughts that fit together?

summaries.example: Suppose Alex believes that the evidence available to Alex strongly supports proposition p, but also believes not-p. This may be epistemic akrasia: a mismatch between a first-order belief and a higher-order belief about what the evidence supports. A wide-scope theory says Alex can restore coherence either by changing the first-order belief or by changing the higher-order assessment. A narrow-scope theory may instead say that once Alex accepts the evidential judgment, rationality specifically requires belief in p. The difference matters because the narrow-scope view can seem to let a person’s own mistaken normative belief generate a requirement to adopt another belief.
summaries.summary: Structural rationality concerns the way a person’s mental states fit together. Paradigm cases include inconsistent beliefs and means-end incoherence: intending an end, believing that a means is necessary, and yet lacking the intention to take that means. Other proposed cases include contradictory intentions, epistemic akrasia, probabilistically incoherent credences, practical akrasia, and cyclical preferences. The entry emphasizes that the status of these cases is often contested. Structural rationality is commonly contrasted with substantive rationality, which concerns responsiveness to reasons. The distinction can be understood in several ways. Some philosophers reserve “rationality” for coherence and treat reasons-responsiveness as a different normative notion. Others argue that the two notions coincide because an agent’s evidence and available reasons are connected to mental states. Still others reduce structural irrationality to failures of substantive rationality, or reduce reasons and substantive rationality to idealized, structurally coherent attitudes. A further option treats the two kinds as genuine and irreducible, while asking how conflicts between them should be handled. The entry surveys debates about structural requirements. Wide-scope requirements prohibit incoherent combinations without specifying which attitude must change; narrow-scope requirements direct revision from one attitude toward another. Requirements may also be synchronic or diachronic, and may govern states or processes of forming and revising attitudes. Skeptics question whether such requirements exist, whether they can be violated, or whether structural irrationality should instead be explained through substantive rationality. key_ideas: Structural rationality usually concerns relations among beliefs, intentions, preferences, or other judgment-sensitive attitudes. The irrationality is often in the combination, not in any single attitude.

Structural assessments can sometimes be made without deciding which individual attitudes are supported by the agent’s reasons. People who disagree about the reasons may still agree that a set of beliefs is inconsistent.
Structural rationality is often described as formal because patterns such as contradiction or means-end conflict can be identified without focusing on the particular content.

The structural/substantive distinction is disputed. Views include identifying rationality with structural coherence, treating the two kinds as equivalent, reducing one to the other, or treating both as genuine and distinct.
Philosophers disagree about the form of rational requirements: wide-scope versus narrow-scope, synchronic versus diachronic, and state requirements versus process requirements.

A central challenge is explaining whether structural rationality is normative. If there are reasons to satisfy structural requirements, some theories seem to generate unacceptable detachment or bootstrapping.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction matters because a person can be criticized for incoherence even when there is disagreement about the person’s evidence, goals, or circumstances. It also prevents a potentially troubling argument: if merely adopting a belief about what one ought to do automatically generated a reason to act on it, mistaken or harmful starting points could produce further reasons. The study of structural rationality therefore connects logic, belief revision, planning, practical reasoning, and theories of reasons. important_terms.definition: The rational status of mental states considered as a fitting or conflicting pattern, rather than assessed one at a time.
Rationality understood as responding appropriately to normative reasons, such as evidence or facts that count in favor of an action or belief.
A mental state that represents or directs a stance, including belief, intention, preference, or desire.
A view on which a requirement governs the whole combination of attitudes, allowing different ways to restore coherence.
A view on which, given one attitude, rationality specifically requires another attitude.
A conflict between a person’s belief about what the evidence supports and the person’s first-order belief.
The problematic idea that adopting one attitude could thereby create a reason or requirement for another, even when the original attitude is misguided.
The claim that a rational assessment can change only when the agent’s mental states change.

questions_to_think_about: If evidence permits more than one belief or credence, can a combination still be structurally irrational?
Should a person resolve an incoherence by changing any one of the conflicting attitudes, or does rationality favor a particular change?
Can a requirement apply across time without unfairly criticizing someone for needing time to revise a belief?
Is coherence valuable in itself, or because it helps with agency, reasoning, interpretation, or another goal?
Does calling someone irrational necessarily imply that the person has a reason to change?

summaries.example: Jordan wants to finish a science project today. Jordan believes that the project cannot be finished without downloading the data, but does not plan to download it. These attitudes form a mismatch. Jordan might change the goal, change the belief about what is needed, or make a plan to download the data. Philosophers debate whether rationality merely requires Jordan to fix the mismatch somehow, or whether it specifically requires the last change.
summaries.summary: Structural rationality is about whether a person’s mental states fit together. Mental states include beliefs, intentions, preferences, and sometimes emotions. A classic example is believing both a claim and its denial. Another is intending a goal, believing that a certain step is necessary for it, and not intending that step. The entry calls such patterns possible cases of structural irrationality. This idea is different from substantive rationality, which asks whether a particular belief or plan responds properly to reasons and evidence. For instance, whether it is sensible for someone to plan medical school may depend on information about costs, chances of success, and interests. By contrast, a means-end mismatch may be visible without knowing much about the person’s situation. Philosophers do not agree on exactly how the two forms of rationality relate. Some treat structural coherence as all there is to rationality; others defend a distinction, identify the two forms, reduce one to the other, or treat both as genuine. They also debate the shape of rational requirements. A wide-scope requirement says that an incoherent combination must be avoided but may allow more than one way to fix it. A narrow-scope requirement says that one attitude requires another. Other debates ask whether requirements apply at one time or across time, and whether they govern mental states or the processes of forming and revising them. Some philosophers even question whether general structural requirements exist. A final question is whether being structurally rational gives us reasons to change our attitudes. The entry presents several proposals and explains why each faces challenges.
key_ideas: Structural rationality usually evaluates combinations of attitudes, not isolated beliefs or plans.
Someone can disagree about the reasons for a belief and still recognize that two beliefs are inconsistent.
Substantive rationality asks about evidence and reasons, so it often depends more on a person’s situation than structural rationality does.
Philosophers disagree about whether structural and substantive rationality are separate, identical, or reducible to one another.
Wide-scope and narrow-scope theories disagree about whether an incoherence can be fixed in several ways or demands one particular change.
The entry also asks whether rationality concerns states, reasoning processes, one moment, or changes across time.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic helps explain why reasoning is not only about having good information. It is also about fitting beliefs, plans, and intentions together. At the same time, it warns us not to confuse consistency with truth or good evidence. A belief can fit neatly with other beliefs and still be unsupported. Understanding this difference can make discussions about disagreement more careful: people may share a judgment about coherence even while disagreeing about evidence or values.

important_terms.definition: When beliefs, intentions, or other mental states fit together instead of pulling against one another.
The kind of rationality concerned with relationships among a person’s mental states.
The kind of rationality concerned with whether a belief or action responds well to reasons and evidence.
A belief, intention, preference, or similar mental stance that can combine with other stances.
A requirement that applies to a whole pattern, so different changes may remove the conflict.
A requirement that starts from one attitude and demands a particular related attitude.
A mismatch between a person’s belief about what they ought to do and their lack of intention to do it.

questions_to_think_about: Can a person’s beliefs be coherent but still poorly supported by evidence?
If someone has a mistaken belief about what they ought to do, should rationality require acting on it?
Is changing a belief always as rational as changing a plan that conflicts with it?
Why might a philosopher think that coherence does not automatically give us a reason?
Can a person reasonably take time to bring their thoughts into agreement?
